Philip IV. From 1268 to 1314, he was called the Fair. He was a centralizing king who challenged papal authority and expanded royal power in France. His reign witnessed the downfall of the Knights Templar, a decisive conflict between state and Church, and the consolidation of Capetian dominance.

During his 29-year reign from 1285 to 1314, Philip aggressively centralized royal authority. He replaced feudal nobles with royal administrators and lawyers loyal to the crown, building a more bureaucratic state apparatus. His ambitions brought him into direct conflict with Pope Boniface VIII over taxation of the clergy and ecclesiastical privileges. This clash marked a watershed moment in the balance of power between state and Church. The conflict signaled that secular authority could challenge the Pope himself and prevail.

Philip's most dramatic act came in 1307 when he arrested and dismantled the Knights Templar. This was a stunning display of royal power against a wealthy, independent order. He seized their vast lands and wealth on charges of heresy. Over the following years from 1307 to 1312, the order was systematically dissolved, and most Templars were executed. The suppression destroyed one of Christendom's great military-religious institutions and filled the royal treasury with their confiscated riches.

Philip also reorganized and strengthened French law and administration, creating a legal framework and government structure that anticipated the modern nation-state. Yet his succession created complications. He married three times and had sons who became kings, but two of his three sons reigned only briefly. Their rapid succession without clear male heirs created succession crises that would shape French history.

His policies toward nobles, the Church, and the Templars presaged the declining power of feudalism and the rising authority of the national monarch. He was the ancestor of all French kings who followed.
